title: Run cost-effective, always-on agents to monitor your environment: the engineering behind Watchers
summary:
Alert rules are great for the failures you can predict, but they fall short on the ones you can't. With the advent of modern AI, you might think the solution is to swarm your stack with agents that monitor every last detail, but that can quickly lead to astronomical bills.

And those are the gaps Watchers fill: catching what alerts miss while keeping costs in control. Generally Available as of ObservabilityCON 2026, Watchers are always-on agents in Grafana Assistant. You describe what to monitor (in natural language) and pick your data sources, and the watcher learns what "normal" looks like and tells you when you drift from that state.

Ultimately, this helps you surface problems without needing an alert, giving you wider coverage and more confidence in your system. But how do we keep Watchers cost-effective for our customers, especially in comparison to building your own agent that runn around the clock?

For example, let's say you deploy your own version of a watcher that checks in every 10 minutes, which means it runs 4,320 times a month. If each run were an agentic investigation, which cost us between $0.56 and $1.26 in a recent experiment, that one watcher you built would cost thousands of dollars a month.

Yet the Watchers running on our own Grafana Cloud stack cost a median of less than $5 a month. In this post, I'll show you the engineering behind that number, which mostly comes down to one question: where do you actually need an LLM's intelligence, and how much of it?

The TL;DR on Watchers

Watchers keeps an eye on one things you care about, such as a service, a dependency, or a fix you shipped after an incident. Think of it as the dashboard check you'd otherwise do by hand, done around the clock. It stays quiet until something needs attention, then it sends you its assessment and the evidence behind it. For critical findings, it can also launch an Investigation in Assistant to find the cause.

Here's the gist of how it helps you identify potential issues in a cost-effective manner, which I'll cover in greater detail in the remaining sections in this post:

  • The design: A capable agent calibrates each watcher once, so every run after that is plain code plus one call to a small, fast model.

  • The cost: Less than $10 a month per watcher for 41 of our 43 internal Watchers. Watchers are free until Dec. 1, 2026, and then will bill as part of Assistant token usage.

  • The results: Coverage beyond your alerts, so you catch what you didn’t know to watch for and better trust your system. Our own watcher found more than 10 customer-affecting production bugs in the past few months.

  • The integrations: Watchers read most of your telemetry, plus any HTTP API, and send findings to Slack, Microsoft Teams, webhooks, or Grafana Alerting.

Put the intelligence only where it's needed

Keeping an eye on a service comes down to three jobs: 

  1. Working out what to watch and what normal looks like

  2. Comparing the same signals with normal again and again

  3. Deciding whether anything is worth interrupting someone for

Only the first and last jobs need intelligence, and they need it in very different amounts. 

Let's go back to our example from the intro about a watcher that checks in every 10 minutes. Determining what to watch takes exploration and judgment, but once you've made a decision, you don't need to revisit it constantly. After all, the answer barely changes between 9 and 9:10 a.m. And deciding whether something matters enough to interrupt someone takes judgment on every run, but it's a narrow question once the legwork is done. The middle job is fetching data and doing arithmetic, which code does well and LLMs don't. 

So a watcher splits the work three ways:

Job

Who does it

When

Decide what to watch and what normal looks like

A calibration agent, with a capable model and tools

Once, and again when you recalibrate

Fetch the data and compare it with the baseline

Plain code: queries, statistics, and log pattern tracking

Every run

Decide whether it matters, and explain why

A small, fast model, in a single call with no tools

Every run

And here's what that workflow looks like:

Calibration: do the hard thinking once

Calibration is the secret sauce. Think of it as pre-processing: when you create a watcher, a background agent does the setup work an experienced engineer would normally do and writes down what it learns. The expensive reasoning happens once, and every run inherits a narrow, well-prepared task that an LLM is good at.

The calibration agent:

  • Settles the scope. It maps where your telemetry lives and asks you up front when it hits a question that only you can answer. For example: "This service runs in 32 production clusters and one ops cluster. Should each cluster be judged on its own?"

  • Starts from what your team knows. It mines your alert rules and dashboards first, since they encode failure modes, thresholds, and severities your team already agreed on.

  • Measures normal over time. It checks each signal at several points over the past week and reads daily and weekly traffic cycles, so a quiet Sunday night doesn't look like an outage.

  • Validates and writes it all down. Every check is tested against live data before it's saved, along with a calibration context: a compact decision guide covering the service, your decisions, deploy behavior, normal ranges, and known noise.

A calibration takes a few minutes at most. Call for call, it's the most expensive thing a watcher does, but it happens once, not every 10 minutes.

Run plain code, then make one model call

A calibrated watcher doesn't explore anything at run time. It executes its saved checks and turns the results into a compact digest, without a model:

  • Metrics: Code compares each value with the same time yesterday and with a statistical baseline, then applies the calibrated thresholds, so the model gets verdicts it can't miscompute.

  • Logs: Loki's patterns API already groups log lines into patterns at ingestion. The watcher keeps an inventory of them across runs, so it can spot new patterns, notice when a known one doubles in rate, and fetch examples only for what's new.

  • Deploys: A check that reports rollouts lets the model tell "this started right after a deploy" from coincidence.

Healthy checks collapse to one line each, and the digest goes to exactly one model call, with no tools. The model returns a structured decision: an assessment (OK, warning, or critical), a short report, the issues it's tracking and their evidence, and whether to notify anyone or launch an investigation.

For example, let's say you roll out a deployment and five minutes later you get an error rate that's slightly up and a log pattern nobody has seen before. Is that noise, or is it worth waking someone up for? This is a task that LLMs are genuinely good at. Weighing evidence like that and explaining the call plays to an LLM's strengths while crunching thousands of data points doesn't. Because the question is this narrow, a small, fast model is enough.

We don't take that on faith, either. Our evals replay real production decisions against candidate models, and the model most watchers use today didn't miss a single critical case, at about half the cost per decision of the model it replaced.

What it costs

Here's what that adds up to for the 43 Watchers running on our internal stack, at our list price of $2 per million tokens:

Types of Watchers

Cost to run per month

Median Watcher

Less than $5

41 of 43 Watchers

Less than $10

Most expensive Watcher (43 checks, every 15 minutes)

A little over $20

Even the most expensive one spends less than one cent per run. Cost follows the two things you control: how often a watcher runs (every five minutes to every three hours) and how much it watches. Calibration comes on top, and investigations a watcher launches are billed as investigations. Each watcher's Overview tab estimates its monthly token usage, so you see the cost before your bill does.

Watchers are free until Dec. 1, 2026. After that, they will draw on your plan’s monthly system-initiated allowance (shared with other automated work) and bill on Assistant token usage. See Grafana Assistant pricing for more info.

Note: Watchers will work exactly as they do today when billing goes live, and we expect the cost of running one to remain in line with what we’ve shared here.

What our own watcher found

A cost-effective watcher is only worth it if it catches things. Over the past few months, the watcher our team runs on Grafana Assistant itself found more than 10 production bugs that affected customers, including:

  • A crashlooping Microsoft Teams integration

  • Broken investigation reports

  • Missing webhook credentials in a newly enabled region

  • Slack OAuth failures

  • Even bugs in Watchers themselves, like alerts that never reached Alertmanager

Many of these surfaced as a new error pattern in the logs. A new pattern alone is often noise, but one that lines up with rising errors and a fresh deploy usually isn't. That's exactly the kind of call a watcher makes well.

It isn't always right about the cause, and it doesn't need to be. During one rollout, it flagged real failures from an exhausted MySQL database but blamed the wrong cause, and engineers found an expensive query plan that likely contributed. The watcher notices; people, or an Assistant Investigation, dig in.

Plug it into your stack

A watcher can sit on top of most of your stack:

  • Data sources: Prometheus (including Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus), CloudWatch metrics, Loki, Tempo, Pyroscope, Synthetic Monitoring, Grafana-managed alerts, and BigQuery for business signals. With the Infinity data source, it can also read any HTTP API that returns JSON or XML. One of ours watches the status pages of the LLM providers that Assistant depends on.

  • Destinations: Slack, Microsoft Teams, signed webhooks, and Grafana Alerting, so findings flow through your notification policies and contact points, including Grafana Cloud IRM. A critical finding can also launch an Assistant Investigation or trigger an Assistant Automation.

Watchers don't replace alert rules; they cover what you can't spell out in advance. To find the right mix, ask Assistant to review a service, and it recommends an alert, a watcher, or both for each failure mode.

To try it, go to AI > Watchers in Grafana Cloud and create a watcher for a service your team checks by hand after every release. Describe what normal looks like, pick your data sources, and let calibration do the rest. To learn more, refer to the Watchers documentation.

title: Any agent anywhere: How to use Grafana Cloud with Claude, Cursor, and any other AI agent
summary:
AI agents are becoming part of everyday engineering workflows, helping teams write code, troubleshoot issues, and automate tasks. But to be truly useful in production, these agents need access to more than code. They also need observability data and context to understand what's happening across your systems, investigate problems, and help you take action.

At Grafana Labs, we believe that context should be available wherever you work. That’s one of the core ideas behind Grafana Cloud as the open agentic observability platform: the flexibility to work with your observability data through the AI agents you prefer—whether it’s Grafana Assistant, a coding agent in your IDE, or a tool you’ve built yourself—so you can investigate and troubleshoot issues without switching tools.

In this post, we'll explore how to bring Grafana Cloud into your agentic workflows using tools like the Grafana Cloud MCP server and gcx, with practical examples along the way. You can also check out our ObservabilityCON 2026 talk in the video below to learn more.

Three ways to use Grafana Cloud with AI agents

There are multiple ways to bring Grafana Cloud observability data and context into your AI workflows, depending on where and how you prefer to work:

  • Work directly in Grafana Cloud: Use Grafana Assistant, the AI-powered assistant built into Grafana Cloud, to investigate issues and interact with your observability data.

  • Connect your preferred AI agent: Use the Grafana Cloud MCP server to bring Grafana Cloud data into compatible tools such as Claude, ChatGPT, and Codex.

  • Work with coding agents and scripts: Use gcx, the Grafana Cloud command-line tool, to give coding agents access to observability data directly from their working environment.

Whether you're working directly in Grafana Cloud with Grafana Assistant or using your own AI agents, you can choose the approach that works best for you. Let's look at how the Grafana Cloud MCP server and gcx make that possible outside of Grafana Cloud.

Investigate an alert from your phone with Claude and Grafana Cloud MCP server

Imagine you're waiting in line at a coffee shop when a Slack message arrives from your director of engineering. Something is wrong with the frontend, and they need your help.

Your laptop is still in your backpack, but you don't necessarily need it to start investigating. With Claude connected to the Grafana Cloud MCP server, you can pull out your phone and ask a simple question: "Why is the frontend slow? Is there anything firing?"

Claude can use Grafana Cloud data to answer your question directly in the conversation. In this example, it confirms that an alert is firing, shows a chart of the relevant signal, and identifies which pages are affected.

You can then ask a follow-up question: how is this affecting the health of the frontend, and what's causing the problem? Again, Claude can return a visual Grafana Cloud view directly in the conversation, giving you more context about the health of your frontend application and helping you determine where to investigate next.

All of this happens without leaving the conversation or opening your laptop. By the time you get your coffee, you've already confirmed the issue and started exploring its impact.

How it works: The Grafana Cloud MCP server and MCP Apps

This experience is powered by two capabilities: the Grafana Cloud MCP server and MCP Apps.

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard that enables AI agents to connect to external tools and data sources. The Grafana Cloud MCP server makes your Grafana Cloud observability data available to compatible agents, allowing them to query alerts, dashboards, and telemetry to help answer questions and investigate issues.

That means you can interact with Grafana Cloud data from the AI tools you already use, rather than rely exclusively on the assistant built into your observability platform.

MCP Apps take this a step further by bringing interactive Grafana Cloud views directly into your AI conversations. Instead of returning only a text description of an issue, an agent can display relevant visualizations, such as firing alerts and frontend health, alongside the conversation.

These views are delivered by the Grafana Cloud MCP server and can appear in MCP clients that support them.

To learn more, see the Grafana Cloud MCP server documentation. 

Continue your investigation in Cursor with Grafana Cloud context and gcx

Now imagine you've grabbed your coffee and opened your laptop. You want to take a closer look at the frontend performance issue and get some help from your coding agent.

You navigate to Grafana Cloud Frontend Observability, where a dashboard shows elevated time to first byte (TTFB), one of the symptoms of the slowdown.

You could manually copy the relevant queries, filters, and time range into your coding agent and explain what you're looking at. But Grafana Cloud provides a simpler way to hand off that context.

From a panel on the dashboard, you can click a button that automatically gathers the relevant information, including the query, filters, and time range. Then you select your agent of choice—Cursor, in this example—and send the context directly to it.

Now Cursor has the same starting context you were using in Grafana Cloud. Instead of explaining the issue from scratch, you can immediately ask it to compare the affected pods with healthy ones. Cursor uses gcx to query Grafana Cloud and begin investigating the differences.

This lets you continue investigating in the environment where you're already working, with the relevant observability context carried over from Grafana Cloud.

How it works: Give coding agents access to Grafana Cloud with gcx

gcx is the Grafana Cloud command-line tool. It provides a way for developers and coding agents to interact with Grafana Cloud directly from a terminal. Because coding agents can execute shell commands, they can also use gcx to access observability data as part of their investigations.

gcx includes curated agent skills that help coding agents understand how to use Grafana Cloud data for common tasks, without requiring step-by-step instructions. Agents can also discover available commands and use them to explore different parts of a system, including services, databases, and frontend sessions.

For example, gcx provides commands to:

  • Explore application services: Inspect services and their operations to understand application behavior.

  • Investigate databases: List and inspect database instances as part of a performance investigation.

  • Examine frontend activity: Access frontend application information and sessions to understand the end-user experience.

Here's an example of available commands, with arguments omitted:

gcx
├─ appo11y
│  ├─ services get
│  └─ services list-operations
├─ dbo11y
│  ├─ instances list
│  └─ instances get
└─ frontend
   ├─ apps list
   └─ sessions get

In our example, gcx gives Cursor a way to look beyond the original alert and query additional observability data to guide its investigation. And because gcx works from the command line, this approach isn't limited to Cursor. Other coding agents that can execute shell commands can use it too, making it possible to incorporate Grafana Cloud data into existing development and automation workflows.

To learn more and get started, visit the gcx repository on GitHub.

Bring it all together: Investigate issues in Slack with an open source agent

What if you'd rather investigate an issue without leaving Slack? You can also connect an open source agent like Hermes to Grafana Cloud using both gcx and the Grafana Cloud MCP server.

For example, imagine your team reports a drop in completed bank transfers, even though traffic looks normal. You can ask Hermes directly in Slack to investigate the issue, providing the affected application, time window, and relevant context.

Hermes can then use gcx commands and MCP tools to investigate the underlying requests, examine user sessions, and compare the results with an earlier time window. From there, it can report its findings back in the Slack thread, with supporting Grafana Cloud links, potential causes, and recommended next steps.

Wrapping up

With Grafana Cloud, you choose the agent, the model, the provider, and where you work. Grafana Cloud then gives your agent access to the observability context and tools it needs to help investigate issues, identify root causes, and take action.

Ready to try it yourself? Here are three ways to get started:

  1. Start with Grafana Assistant to investigate and troubleshoot directly in Grafana Cloud.

  2. Connect your preferred agent through the Grafana Cloud MCP server to bring observability data into compatible AI tools.

  3. Explore gcx to bring Grafana Cloud into your coding agents, scripts, and terminal-based workflows.

│  ├─ services get
│  └─ services list-operations

│  ├─ instances list
│  └─ instances get

With Grafana Cloud, you choose the agent, the model, the provider, and where you work. Grafana Cloud then gives your agent access to the observability context and tools it needs to help investigate issues, identify root causes, and take action.

  2. Connect your preferred agent through the Grafana Cloud MCP server to bring observability data into compatible AI tools.

  3. Explore gcx to bring Grafana Cloud into your coding agents, scripts, and terminal-based workflows.

title: What’s new with Grafana variables: less clutter, easier reuse across dashboards, and more
summary:
Template variables are one of the most used features in Grafana, providing users with a dropdown to turn one dashboard into hundreds: pick a different cluster, region, or service, and every panel updates.

For most of Grafana's history, variables had a single home at the top of the dashboard. Each dashboard had one flat list of variables, and that list was shared by every panel on it. But as dashboards grew in size and number, those controls became harder to organize and maintain. The top of a dashboard could get crowded with dropdowns that only applied to certain panels, while shared controls were copied across dashboards and had to be updated individually.

To address these challenges, we’ve rolled out two new features in Grafana: 

  • Section-level variables for rows and tabs (generally available): these variables let you place controls near the panels they affect, reducing clutter at the top of the dashboard. 

  • Cross-dashboard variables (public preview): these are variables you can define once and reuse across dashboards, keeping configurations consistent and easier to maintain.

In this post, we’ll take a closer look at each variable type, its use cases, and how to get started. 

Section-level variables: define and manage variables by row or tab

Section-level variables let you define variables and filters for a specific row or tab, so they apply only to the panels inside that section. Placing a control next to the panels it affects makes it clear what a selection will change, and it keeps the top of the dashboard uncluttered.

Let’s say you want two $instance dropdowns, one for your API gateway panels and one for your database panels. Traditionally, with one flat namespace, you’d end up with names like $api_instance and $db_instance, or you’d split the dashboard into two.

Now, with section-level variables, the API gateway section and the database section can each have its own $instance variable with its own query and selected value. Both sections still share the dashboard time range, and nothing else on the dashboard changes.

Here’s how section-level variables work:

  • Resolution goes from nearest to farthest. When a panel uses a variable, Grafana first checks the section the panel is in for a matching variable, then any parent sections (rows and tabs can nest), then the dashboard. 

  • Filters work, too. You can add Filter and Group by controls at the section level, so a section can filter by its own labels.

  • The query editor knows about scope. Autocomplete only suggests variables the panel you're editing can actually see.

  • Restructuring is safe. If you ungroup a row or tab, its section variables move up a level instead of disappearing.

To add a section-level variable, edit the dashboard, select a row or tab, and open Variables in the options pane. 

Cross-dashboard variables: define and manage variables across multiple dashboards 

Section variables solved scope inside a dashboard. The bigger request has always been scope across dashboards.

Cross-dashboard variables let you define shared controls once and reuse them across dashboards, reducing duplicate work and keeping configurations consistent.

They come in two scopes:

  • Global variables are defined at the organization level and can be used on any dashboard.

  • Folder variables are defined on a folder and can be used on the dashboards in that folder.

Here's what cross-dashboard variables looks like in practice: say, for example, a few team dashboards all use the same environment picker with the values dev, staging, and prod. With a cross-dashboard variable, you define environment once. When you add a new environment, or change the query behind it, every dashboard that uses the variable gets the update, without needing to edit each dashboard individually.

Cross-dashboard variables achieve this by separating two things: the definition (the variable's type, query, and options) is shared and managed in one place, while the value someone selects (for example, prod) is chosen on each dashboard as they use it.

Managing cross-dashboard variables

Go to Dashboards > Variables to create, edit, move, and delete cross-dashboard variables. The editor is the same one you already use for dashboard variables, with the same types (Query, Custom, Data source, Text, and so on). The only new field is Folder:

  • Leave it at the root to create a global variable.

  • Pick a folder to create a folder variable.

To change a variable's scope, move it between folders or move it to the root.

Choosing variables per dashboard

A dashboard doesn't use any cross-dashboard variables until you choose them. In the dashboard's settings, pick which global and folder variables it should use:

  • Specific variables: only the ones you pick appear on the dashboard. Variables created later in that scope don't appear until you add them.

  • All variables in a scope: every global variable, or every variable in the dashboard's folder, appears. New ones show up automatically.

Precedence: nearest scope wins

With four places a variable can come from, there's one simple rule: the nearest definition wins.

If a dashboard defines its own region, it overrides the global region. A section can override both.

On the dashboard, cross-dashboard variables appear alongside the dashboard's own variables and work the same way: you can select values, sync them to the URL, and use them in queries, titles, and links. In edit mode, they're read-only on the dashboard. To change the definition, go to Dashboards > Variables.

Managing cross-dashboard variables as code

Under the product name, a cross-dashboard variable is a Variable resource with its own API. It isn't stored inside any dashboard, but it is tied to dashboards: it lives in the dashboard API group (dashboard.grafana.app) next to Dashboard, and it does nothing until a dashboard opts into it.

Because it's a separate resource, it's served by the same Kubernetes-style API platform as v2 dashboards and folders. You can create, list, and update variables like any other Grafana resource, without touching a dashboard.

A Variable uses the same shape as a variable inside a dashboard, so anything you already know about dashboard variable JSON carries over:

{
  "apiVersion": "dashboard.grafana.app/v2beta1",
  "kind": "Variable",
  "metadata": {
    "annotations": {
      "grafana.app/folder": ""
    }
  },
  "spec": {
    "kind": "CustomVariable",
    "spec": {
      "name": "environment",
      "query": "dev,staging,prod",
      "current": { "text": "prod", "value": "prod" },
      "description": "Deployment environment"
    }
  }
}

Leave out the grafana.app/folder annotation to make it global.

During the public preview, Variable is served at v2beta1.  It will move to v2 when cross-dashboard variables reach general availability.

Provisioning with Terraform

Because Variable is a standard API resource, you can manage it with the Grafana Terraform provider's grafana_apps_generic_resource. Here's a folder, a folder variable, and a dashboard that opts into it, all in one Terraform configuration:

resource "grafana_apps_generic_resource" "payments_folder" {
  manifest = {
    apiVersion = "folder.grafana.app/v1"
    kind       = "Folder"
    metadata   = { name = "payments" }
    spec       = { title = "Payments" }
  }
}

resource "grafana_apps_generic_resource" "payments_env" {
  manifest = {
    apiVersion = "dashboard.grafana.app/v2beta1"
    kind       = "Variable"
    metadata = {
      annotations = {
        "grafana.app/folder" = "payments"
      }
    }
    spec = {
      kind = "CustomVariable"
      spec = {
        name    = "environment"
        query   = "dev,staging,prod"
        current = { text = "prod", value = "prod" }
      }
    }
  }

  depends_on = [grafana_apps_generic_resource.payments_folder]
}

resource "grafana_apps_generic_resource" "payments_overview" {
  manifest = {
    apiVersion = "dashboard.grafana.app/v2"
    kind       = "Dashboard"
    metadata = {
      name = "payments-overview"
      annotations = {
        "grafana.app/folder"                     = "payments"
        "grafana.app/useCrossDashboardVariables" = jsonencode({
          global = ["region"]
          folder = ["environment"]
        })
      }
    }
    spec = {
      title = "Payments overview"
      # ... panels and layout
    }
  }

  depends_on = [grafana_apps_generic_resource.payments_env]
}

The opt-in setting also works naturally as code. Leave out the annotation, and the dashboard uses no cross-dashboard variables. List names, and it uses exactly those. Nothing appears on a provisioned dashboard unless the config says so.

The same API also works with kubectl, curl, or any tool that talks to Grafana's /apis endpoints.

Wrapping up

These updates mean Grafana variables have one consistent model, from a single section of a dashboard to your whole organization:

Variable scope

Defined on

Stored in

Applies to

Section

A row or tab

The dashboard (v2 schema)

Panels in that section

Dashboard

The dashboard

The dashboard (v2 schema)

The whole dashboard

Folder

A folder

Its own Variable resource

Opted-in dashboards in the folder

Global

The stack

Its own Variable resource

Opted-in dashboards anywhere

The result is less clutter where you build dashboards, and less copy-and-paste where you maintain them.

Here are two quick ways to get started:

  1. Give two sections of a dashboard their own controls. Edit a dashboard, select a row or tab, and open Variables in the options pane. Add an instance variable to each section and see how each one only affects its own panels.

  2. Share a variable across a few dashboards. Go to Dashboards > Variables and create a variable such as environment. Then open the settings for two or three dashboards and choose it under cross-dashboard variables.

To learn more, see the docs for section-level variables and cross-dashboard variables. We'd love to hear how you use them. Please reach out in our Community Slack.

title: Bridging Alloy and OpenTelemetry: the OTel engine is now in Public Preview
summary:
Many Grafana Cloud customers love what Alloy offers them, but we're also seeing a growing base of users who feel the same way about the OpenTelemetry Collector. We want to make it easy for customers to make the decision that makes the most sense, regardless of their preference.

When we introduced the OpenTelemetry engine for Grafana Alloy, we set out to give teams a way to run native OTLP pipelines without giving up the power and flexibility Alloy is known for. Since then we've kept building: ironing out service installation support, enabling Fleet Management, and folding in feedback from early users. Today, as of Alloy v1.21.0, we're happy to share that the OTel engine has moved into Public Preview, running right alongside the default engine you already know. 

In this post, we'll dig into when you'd reach for each engine, walk through some of the most interesting use cases we've seen so far, and give a preview of where both engines are headed next.

The motivation behind each engine

Before diving into specific new features, let’s recap why we have two engines in Alloy.

Default engine

The default engine is a cross-ecosystem engine at its core; it's not tied to any single wire format or vendor. It can just as easily run a Prometheus pipeline, an OTLP pipeline, or a Loki pipeline, all defined using Alloy's own configuration syntax. That flexibility is what makes it a Swiss army knife: the same engine that scrapes Prometheus metrics can pull in logs over syslog for logs, ingest OTLP, scrape Prometheus metrics from embedded exporters, and route all of it to wherever it needs to go.

OpenTelemetry engine 

There's a lot to like about being able to speak every ecosystem's language. But the telemetry landscape itself is moving in the opposite direction. Rather than translating between formats, the industry is increasingly converging on a single, shared model defined by the OpenTelemetry specification. That's what an OpenTelemetry Collector actually is: a pipeline that treats OTLP as the native format end-to-end, prioritizing portability and open standards over ecosystem-bridging translation. At its core, Alloy's OTel engine is Grafana Labs' own distribution of the OpenTelemetry Collector.

Running the OTel engine

It's just a collector

The OTel engine is an OpenTelemetry Collector distribution that ships inside Alloy. It runs standard collector YAML with no translation and no Alloy syntax. If you already have a collector config, you already have an OTel engine config.

- otelcol --config=config.yaml
+ alloy otel --config=config.yaml

The rest of the CLI matches, too. validate, components, print-config, and --set all work the way they do upstream, so scripts and CI that call otelcol validate keep working.

The same goes for the tools you deploy collectors with. On the upstream Helm chart, it's two values:

image:
  repository: grafana/alloy
command:
  name: "bin/otelcol"

The OpenTelemetry Operator used to fail on the Alloy image because it had no way to set the container command. We added spec.command upstream (Operator v0.153.0 and later), so now it's one line:

spec:
  image: grafana/alloy:
  command: ["/bin/alloy", "otel"]

For a non-containerized installation, the Alloy packages can run either engine as a service. Set ALLOY_OTEL_MODE=1 and the service runs the OTel engine against config.yaml. Read our docs for more information on how to set it up by platform.

Fleet management

Managing collector configuration by hand doesn't scale past a handful of hosts, so remote configuration was one of the first gaps we closed after the initial release. As of Alloy v1.19.0, you can manage OTel engine configuration centrally with Fleet Management. The OpAMP supervisor is embedded in the Alloy binary and runs through the new experimental otel-supervisor subcommand: point it at your Fleet Management endpoint and credentials with a supervisor configuration file, and Alloy handles the connection, pulls down your pipeline configuration, and applies changes as you publish them. See the Alloy otel-supervisor reference to get started.

An escape hatch: the alloyengine extension

Sometimes the component you need only exists in the default engine today. The alloyengine extension runs Alloy configuration inside the same collector process, so you can pick up that one piece without running a second agent.

It's Experimental, and we expect it to stay that way. The two engines run side by side but can't pass data to each other directly, so anything that crosses over goes out over the network, usually OTLP.

If you reach for it, tell us why. Open an issue on the Alloy repo with the component you needed. That list is how we decide which default engine pieces become native OpenTelemetry collector components next.

Experiments with Grafana Cloud products

Heads up first: nothing in this section is supported, and you shouldn't run it in production. Part of what we're working out with the OTel engine is how Grafana Cloud's products behave when the pipeline is OTel end to end. Here's where two of them stand.

Database Observability. Today the path that works is adding your existing Alloy config to the collector you already run. Your OTLP pipelines keep doing their thing, and the extension runs database observability next to them. The Database Observability app can't tell the difference:

extensions:
  alloyengine:
    config:
      inline:
        content: |
          database_observability.postgres "default" {
            data_source_name = env("POSTGRES_DSN")
            forward_to       = [loki.write.grafana_cloud.receiver]
          }
          // ...the rest of your existing Alloy config

receivers:
  otlp:
    protocols:
      grpc: {}
      http: {}

service:
  extensions: [alloyengine]
  pipelines:
    traces:
      receivers: [otlp]
      exporters: [otlp_http/grafana_cloud]

A native collector path is in the works but still further off as we decide how to break the Alloy components out into OpenTelemetry native ones.

Cloud Provider Observability. Alloy's cloud provider exporters, like prometheus.exporter.gcp, work through the extension the same way. The data will be identical when run in the alloyengine extension as when run in Alloy’s default engine. The more interesting result is what happens without Alloy’s native Prometheus exporters at all. 

We've been working with the Prometheus community to make exporters embeddable as libraries, so they run as real collector receivers instead of something a collector scrapes. With a collector built to include it, the GCP exporter is just another receiver:

receivers:
  stackdriver_exporter:
    exporter_config:
      project_ids: [""]
      metrics_prefixes: [compute.googleapis.com/instance]
      aggregate_deltas: true  # off by default; Alloy turns it on

Looking beyond Cloud Provider Observability, the OpenTelemetry Collector Prometheus Distro is an official, experimental collector distribution that ships embeddable Prometheus exporters as OpenTelemetry receivers including blackbox, Postgres, Google Cloud Monitoring with stackdriver exporter and CloudWatch through yet-another-cloudwatch exporter. The receivers live in prometheus-opentelemetry-collector if you'd rather build your own with Open Telemetry Collector Builder (OCB). As they progress through the OpenTelemetry stability model we will look to add them to the OTel engine.

Looking ahead

OTel engine

So what comes next for the OTel engine now that it's in Public Preview? Making sure you can properly debug your collector is high on the list. Support bundles are a key feature for this in the default engine —a single request to /-/support packages your configuration, logs, internal metrics, runtime flags, and pprof profiles into one file you can inspect before sharing. image:
  repository: grafana/alloy
command:
  name: "bin/otelcol"

spec:
  image: grafana/alloy:
  command: ["/bin/alloy", "otel"]

title: Trace linkage: connect the dots between your app traces and database queries
summary:
When an application request slows down, a trace can show a database call. Finding the database query behind it can be tedious, requiring you to switch between traces and database telemetry, as well as match timestamps or query text by hand. 

In Grafana Cloud, the Database Observability app already provides a window into all of your database telemetry, including query samples, performance history, and explain plan. But what if you could jump from that database call in the trace straight to its query details?

OpenTelemetry database semantic conventions stabilized last year, giving us all a dependable shared language for describing database operations. That foundation has opened the door for what we call trace linkage, now Generally Available in Database Observability!

What is trace linkage?

With trace linkage, we try to provide a connection between OpenTelemetry-instrumented applications and database telemetry collected with Alloy. In other words, when you give us these previously-disjoint puzzle pieces, we’ll do our best to provide you as much supporting information between these two elements as we can. And we'll do it without making you tediously piece together timestamps and logs. 

From a database span in a trace, you’ll see a link on the query text. Clicking from there, the app searches for a connection between your database query and our opinionated view of your most relevant data in the Database Observability app. You can explore sampled query execution data or check out the query’s historical performance, alongside that query’s related schema and explain plan.

This connection builds on the database attributes your OpenTelemetry instrumentation already emits. Grafana Cloud Traces, powered by Tempo, retain those attributes, and trace linkage uses the query text, database system, and database name to connect a database span to its supporting query context in Database Observability. 

We support the stable conventions like db.query.text and its legacy equivalent db.statement, so existing instrumentation can continue to benefit as teams adopt the stable conventions.

How does it work?

The initial idea for trace linkage came from this question: What shared context could connect application instrumentation with telemetry collected from the database?

The answer was to leverage trace context: the trace ID and span ID. On one side we have an application trace with spans representing a query execution. On the Database Observability side, we are collecting telemetry from the database concerning query executions. As long as the telemetry we collect contains the same trace ID and span ID, we can make a link between the application trace and Database Observability. 

This led us to sqlcommenter, an open source project donated to the OpenTelemetry community. Its idea is (delightfully) simple: let the SQL statement carry a piece of trace context with it in a comment. With trace context propagation enabled, sqlcommenter injects the application’s trace ID and span ID into a comment at the end of the SQL statement. This is done at the level of an individual query execution, so this is like a shared thread that allows us to follow from a trace span to a specific query execution.

We then search the trace ID and span ID in the logs that we generated in the Database Observability Alloy component: our component extracts traceparent from the SQL comment and includes it in query sample logs.

Going beyond a traceparent match

However, having sqlcommenter enabled doesn’t guarantee that Alloy captured the particular SQL execution. That can depend on how short-lived a query may be or how often Alloy polls the database. Even if you are ready to use sqlcommenter, not every database engine is supported, and it can come with downsides for database caches. This means that you might have traces for which we can’t find a query sample in Database Observability, at least not with sqlcommenter exclusively.

We can go beyond sqlcommenter-based matching by using the query statement itself. When we can’t find an exact match, we look for matching query text in the telemetry collected by Alloy.

That sounds straightforward, but the same query can look different on each side. OpenTelemetry instrumentation doesn’t always record statements in the same way: depending on the language and instrumentation used, literal values may be preserved or masked, and parameter placeholders can take different forms. Meanwhile, database engines apply their own normalization to the query text that Alloy collects. We account for these differences, along with formatting and comments, to find a match.

Even when we can’t point you to the exact execution, you can still explore the samples and historical performance we’ve gathered for that query! This lets us make a meaningful link between your traces and Database Observability, even without sqlcommenter.

Start with query text matching, then use sqlcommenter to match trace and span IDs exactly

Trace linkage can be a great tool for quickly connecting your database and application telemetry, so we're excited for you to try it today. If your application is already instrumented as an OpenTelemetry SDK that sends traces to Grafana Cloud and you’ve already set up Database Observability, then read our docs about setting up trace linkage to help you get started. 

If Database Observability has collected a query and the database span already includes its text in db.query.text or the legacy db.statement, chances are trace linkage can already match the span to that query without further application instrumentation.

Once you’ve tried query text matching, you can optionally go beyond and match a trace to a specific query execution with the use of sqlcommenter, as this blog discussed extensively. This improves match precision; exact matches remain best-effort because Alloy may not sample that execution.

And if you aren't sure where to start, ask Grafana Assistant for help, using natural language.

title: Instrumentation Hub in Grafana Cloud: start easier, stay in control
summary:
It's no secret that getting started with observability can be much harder than it should be. That's why, at ObservabilityCon 2025, we introduced Instrumentation Hub: a guided, scalable way to roll out observability coverage while still keeping you in control. 

Today, we’re excited to announce that Instrumentation Hub is now Generally Available in Grafana Cloud.

As we hinted at before, this new iteration introduces selective OpenTelemetry SDK injection, giving you deeper runtime insights for a wide range of languages to complement eBPF instrumentation with a single click. 

What is the Instrumentation Hub?

Instrumentation Hub makes the biggest bottleneck of starting with observability, instrumentation, faster and easier by leveraging open source eBPF and OTel injection.

At Grafana Labs, we're champions of open-standards-based observability, but we also realize that getting meaningful coverage of your systems can often mean months of manual toil. Each layer requires its own instrumentation approach, balancing technology tradeoffs, and unique brittle steps. 

Organizational challenges exacerbate this process, making observability a moving target with uneven coverage, persistent blind spots, and ultimately leaving you wondering if the effort was worth the pain.

We believe there’s a better way. Instrumentation Hub is a control plane for remote discovery and selective auto-instrumentation. It helps you go from zero to meaningful telemetry in a matter of minutes by removing the bottleneck of having to apply instrumentation by hand.

How Instrumentation Hub works

The premise is simple: you run a single Helm command on your Kubernetes cluster to install Alloy, our distribution of the OpenTelemetry Collector.

Once installed, Instrumentation Hub automatically catalogs everything that’s running on the cluster, structured by namespace and technology. Teams can immediately see what exists, what’s instrumented, and what isn’t.

Then, you use either the Grafana Cloud UI, an API automation, or your favorite LLM agent to describe what and how you want to collect and monitor.

Under the hood, Instrumentation Hub translates these selections into observability pipelines without the need for manual configuration. Within minutes you can begin exploring insights across your infrastructure and services in the Grafana Cloud observability platform.

And of course, this isn’t a one-time setup. Teams can come back any time and refine their observability scope by namespace and enable or disable specific signal collection to balance their observability budgets. Need profiles for a misbehaving service? Enable them temporarily. Too many logs from a noisy workload? Exclude them. Trying to reduce spend? Dial back collection where it’s no longer needed.

Observability is a progression

Last year at ObservabilityCon, we introduced the idea of a hierarchy of observability needs as a mental model to chart an effective path for applying observability. We described how you should start from a bird’s eye view of your estate and gradually move towards deeper and more customized insights.

Instrumentation Hub is built around this progression, facilitating observability in the right order for a maximum return on investment.

At the base is the foundation everything depends on: infrastructure visibility, which provides insight into the machines the code runs on. Instrumentation Hub helps you get started at this layer by enabling Kubernetes Monitoring with the click of a button.

Above infrastructure is baseline service visibility. RED metrics and service relationships provide a consistent, system-wide view so teams can quickly triage issues and narrow the search space before digging deeper. Instrumentation Hub populates Grafana Cloud's Knowledge Graph in a matter of minutes, providing rich context for humans and agents.

At the next level, technology-specific and transaction-level insights become necessary. Distributed traces reveal application behavior across the full request path, exposing performance bottlenecks and dependencies that aren’t visible from the outside.

This is where Instrumentation Hub stands out. It can selectively deploy OpenTelemetry auto-instrumentation SDKs with the click of a button.

Historically, this process meant installing a new Operator, deploying instrumentation CRDs, annotating your target applications, and restarting the pods. This work can span across multiple teams, ownership boundaries, or require a dedicated new collection layer. But now, the very same upstream SDKs can be rolled out to complement and enrich your existing baseline service visibility without any extra moving pieces and without disruptive restarts.

Get started with Instrumentation Hub today

Try it out! The Instrumentation Hub is available to all Grafana Cloud stacks for your Kubernetes clusters running on Linux.

If you’ve recently installed the Kubernetes Monitoring Helm chart you might be set up with it already. And if you're still unsure, ask Grafana Assistant for help!

title: Grafana 13.3 release: manage variables across dashboards, share findings with Notebooks, a UI refresh, and more
summary:
Grafana 13.3 is here, bringing more consistency and control to how you work across Grafana. 

Cross-dashboard variables help you manage shared dashboard controls from one place, while Notebooks let you capture and share findings from across Grafana in a single, editable document. You'll also get a first look at Grafana's biggest visual refresh since Grafana 7, along with new ways to guide and refine dashboards built with Grafana Assistant.

Below are just some of the highlights from this release. You can explore all of the updates in the changelog or our What's new in Grafana 13.3 documentation.

Define a variable once and use it across dashboards

Available in public preview in all editions of Grafana

You can create and manage these variables from Dashboards > Variables, and scope each one as either:

  • Global: available to every dashboard in the organization

  • Folder: available only to dashboards in the same folder

Available in public preview in all editions of Grafana

An investigation rarely happens in one place. You might start on a dashboard panel, jump into Explore to run a query, and then ask Grafana Assistant what's going on. Until now, the evidence and your reasoning ended up scattered across tabs, screenshots, and chat threads.

Notebooks let you capture findings from across Grafana in a single, editable document. Add panels from dashboards or Explore, pull in findings from Grafana Assistant, and write your observations right next to the data. Teammates can then follow your investigation, understand how you reached your conclusions, and collaborate on next steps.

You can use a notebook to:

  • Explore a question about your data, keeping queries and notes side by side as your thinking develops.

  • Document an investigation so the next person doesn't have to start from scratch.

  • Prepare a post-incident review with the relevant panels already in place.

Available in public preview in all editions of Grafana

Whether it’s adding new data sources or supporting new use cases, we’re constantly expanding what Grafana can do. And as AI-powered workflows with Grafana Assistant became a bigger part of how people use Grafana every day, we saw an opportunity to rethink how the platform looks and feels.

With Grafana 13.3, we're introducing the first phase of our biggest visual refresh since Grafana 7. Built on an updated set of design principles, the refresh introduces new colors, typography, and UI components to create a more modern, consistent experience across Grafana.

Updates include: 

  • New default dark and light themes. We've reworked every theme color, with more shades for flexibility, and main action buttons now have a solid, high-contrast style.

  • Softer borders and floating components. Rounder corners offer a more modern feel, and subtle borders on cards, panels, and drawers create a clearer sense of depth. The toolbar and navigation also stand apart more clearly from page content.

  • Updated inputs, drop-downs, buttons, and tags. We've resized our most-used components to be more proportional and consistent. 

  • Revised typography. A new type scale mixes font weights and sizes, rather than relying on size alone, so it's easier to see what matters most on a page. 

Importantly, this is a visual refresh, not a redesign. Your existing workflows and navigation stay the same, and there are no breaking changes for plugins. Plugins that use standard Grafana components and theme tokens will automatically pick up the new look, while those with custom styling can migrate on their own timeline.

To try out the new UI in self-managed Grafana, enable the grafana.visualDesignRefresh feature toggle. You can switch back to the previous design at any time, and we welcome your feedback as we continue rolling out improvements over the coming months.

Grafana Assistant can already help you build and edit dashboards from a plain-language description. Now, with Grafana 13.3, you have more control over that process, from reviewing and refining a dashboard plan before it's built to easily undoing changes afterward. 

Review a dashboard plan from Assistant

Available in public preview in all editions of Grafana 

With dashboard plans, you can describe what you want to monitor, and instead of building it right away, Assistant proposes a plan in chat. The plan covers the dashboard title, tabs or rows, panels, visualization types, and variables, so you can catch a missing panel or the wrong chart type before anything is built.

Select Preview to open a read-only version of the dashboard, then keep the conversation going to iterate from there. When the preview matches what you need, select Build it to generate the dashboard and save it.

Generally available in all editions of Grafana 

Experimenting with different layouts and visualizations is easier when you can quickly undo changes you don’t want. With Grafana 13.3, you can now select Undo turn after Grafana Assistant edits your dashboard to restore it to its previous state. If Assistant changed multiple panels in a single request, you can undo all those changes at once.

To learn more, refer to the Grafana Assistant dashboarding guide.

More to explore in Grafana 13.3

Beyond these highlights, Grafana 13.3 includes a range of updates related to data visualization, alerting, Git Sync, and more. 

For an in-depth list of all the new features, check out our Grafana documentation, the Grafana changelog, or our What's New documentation.
